schema.volatile: figure may change; re-check by review_by

questions.question: How long does a full switch with the Current Account Switch Service (CASS) take?
questions.explanation: A full CASS switch takes 7 working days, and you choose the switch date.

questions.question: How much does it cost a customer to use CASS?
options: A fee taken later by your new bank
questions.explanation: CASS is free for customers.

questions.question: What does the Current Account Switch Guarantee promise?
options: Your new bank will pay you a bonus
Interest and charges caused by a failed switch are refunded
questions.explanation: If anything goes wrong with the switch, the Guarantee means interest and charges caused by it are refunded.

questions.question: After a full CASS switch, payments sent to your old account details are…
options: Frozen until you call your old bank
questions.explanation: CASS redirects payments sent to your old details, so nothing gets lost.

questions.question: A “full switch” with CASS means…
options: Your old account closes and everything moves to the new one
You keep both accounts and copy some payments
questions.explanation: In a full switch, payments move across and the old account closes.

questions.question: Why do most bank switch bonuses need a FULL switch, not a partial one?
options: The bonus terms usually say so: the bank wants your whole account
questions.explanation: Switch bonuses usually require a full CASS switch. A partial switch typically won't qualify.

questions.question: A switch offer says “pay in £1,000”. Usually that means…
options: Deposit at least £1,000 within the deadline, often from an external account
questions.explanation: It's a deposit requirement, usually within a time limit. Check whether transfers between your own accounts at that bank count.

questions.question: A switch offer needs 2 active Direct Debits. What does “active” usually mean?
options: Set up, even if not yet collected
At least one payment has actually been collected
questions.explanation: Active usually means at least one payment has gone out. Set Direct Debits up early.

questions.question: Many switch offers exclude you if, in a set period, you've had…
options: A previous switch bonus or account with that same bank
questions.explanation: Eligibility rules often exclude recent customers or previous bonus claimants of the same bank (or bank group).

questions.question: What's a “clawback” in an offer's terms?
options: The bank taking the bonus back if you break the conditions, e.g. closing the account early
questions.explanation: Some offers can reclaim the bonus if you close the account or break the terms within a set period.

questions.question: What is a Direct Debit?
options: A payment you push yourself each time
An instruction letting a company collect payments, which can vary, from your account
questions.explanation: A Direct Debit lets an organisation collect money from your account. The amount can change, but you must be told in advance.

questions.question: Direct Debit vs standing order: what's the key difference?
options: You set and control a standing order; a Direct Debit is collected by the company and can vary
Standing orders are only for businesses
questions.explanation: You control a standing order's amount and dates. A Direct Debit is pulled by the company.

questions.question: The Direct Debit Guarantee means…
options: You get an immediate refund from your bank if a payment is taken in error
Your bank pays your bills if you can't
questions.explanation: If an error is made, your bank must refund you straight away.

questions.question: Since 2020, UK overdrafts are mostly charged as…
questions.explanation: FCA rules banned fixed daily and monthly overdraft fees. Overdrafts are now priced with a simple interest rate.

questions.question: Compared with an arranged overdraft, an unarranged overdraft's rate can be…
questions.explanation: FCA rules stop banks charging more for unarranged overdrafts than arranged ones.

questions.question: A sort code identifies…
questions.explanation: The sort code identifies the bank and branch. The account number identifies your account.

questions.question: Why does a bank check your ID when you open an account?
questions.explanation: Banks must verify who their customers are under anti-money-laundering rules.

questions.question: Your overdraft rate is 39.9% EAR. Roughly what does staying £500 overdrawn for a whole year cost?
questions.explanation: 39.9% of £500 is about £200 a year.

questions.question: What is Confirmation of Payee?
options: A check that the name you enter matches the account you're paying
questions.explanation: It warns you if the name doesn't match the account, which helps stop mistakes and scams.

questions.question: Before switching your only current account for a bonus, what's a sensible safeguard?
options: Open a second account to switch from, so your salary and bills aren't disrupted
Cancel all your Direct Debits first
questions.explanation: Many hunters keep a spare account just for switching, so their main money never moves.

questions.question: When you apply for a new current account, the bank…
options: Often runs a hard search, especially if there's an overdraft, which shows on your file
questions.explanation: Many current account applications involve a hard credit search. Space applications out if you're planning a mortgage.

questions.question: What does AER stand for on a savings account?
questions.explanation: AER shows what you'd earn over a year, including compounding.

questions.question: Why use AER to compare savings accounts?
options: It includes compounding, so accounts compare fairly
questions.explanation: AER puts accounts with different interest payment schedules on a level footing.

questions.question: Easy-access vs fixed-term savings: what's the usual trade-off?
options: Fixed usually pays more but locks your money away
questions.explanation: Fixed-term accounts often pay more in exchange for tying your money up.

questions.question: Account A pays 5% on the first £1,000 and 1% on the rest. Account B pays 4% on everything. With £5,000 for a year, which earns more?
questions.explanation: A: £50 + £40 = £90. B: £200. The headline rate isn't the whole story.

questions.question: A regular saver account typically…
options: Lets you pay in a limited amount each month at a higher rate
questions.explanation: Regular savers cap monthly deposits, often with a higher rate.

questions.question: A regular saver pays 6% AER. You pay in £200 a month for 12 months. Roughly how much interest do you earn?
questions.explanation: 6% of the final £2,400 is £144, but the money isn't all there for the whole year. Your average balance is about £1,300, so you earn roughly £78.

questions.question: What is an emergency fund?
options: Money set aside for surprises like a broken boiler or job loss
questions.explanation: It's a cash buffer so surprises don't push you into debt.

questions.question: A common guideline for an emergency fund is…
questions.explanation: Many guides suggest 3–6 months of essential costs, built up gradually.

questions.question: The FSCS protects eligible savings per person, per…
questions.explanation: Protection works per banking licence, so brands sharing a licence share one limit.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT protected by the FSCS?
options: A current account at a UK-authorised bank
Money held on a crypto exchange
questions.explanation: Crypto isn't FSCS protected.

questions.question: Two bank brands share one banking licence and you have savings in both. Under the FSCS…
options: They share a single protection limit
questions.explanation: Check which brands share a licence before spreading large sums around.

questions.question: Instead of interest, Premium Bonds give you…
questions.explanation: Each £1 bond is entered into a monthly prize draw.

questions.question: Premium Bonds are backed by…
questions.explanation: NS&I is backed by HM Treasury.

questions.question: Premium Bond prizes are…
questions.explanation: Prizes are tax-free.

questions.question: Interest earned in a Cash ISA is…
questions.explanation: ISA interest is tax-free.

questions.question: How much can you pay into ISAs in total in the 2026/27 tax year?
questions.explanation: The overall ISA allowance is £20,000, split across your ISAs however you like.
questions.verify: Overall ISA allowance and any Cash ISA limit changes on gov.uk

questions.question: You take £1,000 out of a standard (non-flexible) Cash ISA, then put it back in the same tax year. What happens?
options: Putting it back uses up more of your allowance
questions.explanation: With a non-flexible ISA, money paid back counts as a new subscription. Flexible ISAs work differently.

questions.question: Inflation is 4% and your savings earn 2%. In real terms your money is…
options: Losing about 2% of its buying power a year
questions.explanation: Prices are rising faster than your interest.

questions.question: Same gross rate: interest paid monthly vs annually. Which grows slightly more if you leave the interest in?
questions.explanation: Monthly interest starts earning interest sooner, so it grows slightly more.

questions.question: Profits inside a Stocks & Shares ISA are…
questions.explanation: Gains and dividends inside an ISA are tax-free.

questions.question: Which of these is generally lower risk?
questions.explanation: A global index fund spreads your money across thousands of companies.

questions.question: A trading app gives you a free share. Before you sell it, check…
options: Any minimum holding period in the terms
questions.explanation: Many free-share offers require you to keep the share, or the account, for a set time.

questions.question: Using the Rule of 72, at 6% a year, roughly how long does money take to double?
Fund A charges 1.5% a year, Fund B 0.2%. On £10,000, how much more does A cost per year?
questions.explanation: 1.3% of £10,000 = £130 a year, and the gap compounds over time.

questions.question: £2,000 grows by 7% a year, compounded yearly. Roughly how much after 10 years?
questions.explanation: £2,000 × 1.07¹⁰ ≈ £3,934. Simple interest would only give £3,400.

questions.question: Diversification means…
options: Putting everything in one hot stock
questions.explanation: Spreading your money means one bad pick can't sink you.

questions.question: An index fund aims to…
options: Beat the market by picking winners
Track a market index like the FTSE 100
questions.explanation: Index funds track a market rather than trying to beat it, which usually keeps fees low.

questions.question: Why do long-term investors often sit tight through short-term drops?
options: Markets have historically recovered over long periods, though nothing is guaranteed
questions.explanation: History favours patience, but past performance isn't a guarantee.

questions.question: “Investments can go down as well as up” means…
options: You could get back less than you put in
questions.explanation: Investing carries the risk of losing money.

questions.question: A dividend is…
options: Part of a company's profits paid to shareholders
questions.explanation: Companies may share profits with shareholders as dividends.

questions.question: Pound-cost averaging means…
options: Investing a fixed amount regularly, buying more when prices are low
questions.explanation: Regular investing smooths out the price you pay.

questions.question: Your fund rises 10%, then falls 10%. Overall you are…
Is crypto held on an exchange covered by the FSCS?
questions.explanation: Crypto isn't FSCS protected. If an exchange fails, you could lose everything.

questions.question: Who regulates most UK investment firms?
questions.explanation: The Financial Conduct Authority regulates investment firms. Check the FCA Register before investing.

questions.question: A platform charges 0.45% a year. On £20,000, that's…
An investment promising “guaranteed 20% a month” is…
questions.explanation: Guaranteed high returns are the classic scam promise.

questions.question: A Stocks & Shares ISA protects you from…
questions.explanation: An ISA is a tax wrapper. Your investments can still fall.

questions.question: Your investments grow 6% in a year when inflation is 4%. Your real return is roughly…
questions.explanation: Real return ≈ 6% − 4% = 2%.

questions.question: Before investing, many guides suggest you first…
options: Build an emergency fund and clear expensive debt
questions.explanation: Expensive debt usually costs more than investments earn, and a buffer stops you selling at a bad time.

questions.question: The UK tax year runs from…
questions.explanation: The tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April.

questions.question: The standard Personal Allowance (income you can earn tax-free) is…
questions.explanation: The standard Personal Allowance is £12,570. It's reduced for very high earners.

questions.question: How much savings interest can a basic-rate taxpayer earn tax-free (Personal Savings Allowance)?
questions.explanation: Basic-rate taxpayers get £1,000. Higher-rate taxpayers get £500.

questions.question: The Personal Savings Allowance for a higher-rate taxpayer is…
questions.explanation: Higher-rate taxpayers get £500. Additional-rate taxpayers get nothing.

questions.question: HMRC's trading allowance lets you earn how much a year in side income before you need to tell them?
questions.explanation: The trading allowance covers up to £1,000 of gross trading income.

questions.question: Selling your own old clothes online for less than you paid is usually…
options: Not trading, so normally no tax
questions.explanation: Selling personal belongings isn't trading. Buying items to resell for profit is.

questions.question: Online marketplaces now share seller details with HMRC once you sell around…
options: 30 items, or about £1,700, in a year
questions.explanation: Platforms report sellers who hit 30 sales or about £1,700 a year. Reporting isn't the same as owing tax.
questions.verify: Digital platform reporting thresholds on gov.uk

questions.question: The deadline for filing an online Self Assessment tax return is…
options: 31 January after the tax year ends
questions.explanation: Online returns are due by 31 January after the end of the tax year.

questions.question: The dividend allowance (2026/27) is…
questions.explanation: You can earn £500 of dividends tax-free outside an ISA.

questions.question: The Capital Gains Tax annual exempt amount is…
questions.explanation: You can make £3,000 of gains a year tax-free outside an ISA.
questions.verify: CGT annual exempt amount on gov.uk

questions.question: Marriage Allowance lets a lower earner transfer…
options: £1,260 of their Personal Allowance to a basic-rate partner
questions.explanation: Eligible couples can transfer £1,260, which saves up to £252 a year.

questions.question: Does Cash ISA interest use up your Personal Savings Allowance?
options: No: ISA interest is tax-free and separate
questions.explanation: ISA interest doesn't count towards your Personal Savings Allowance.

questions.question: Your tax code tells your employer…
options: How much tax-free pay you get
questions.explanation: The tax code reflects your allowances so the right tax is taken.

questions.question: National Insurance contributions build up your entitlement to…
questions.explanation: Your NI record decides your State Pension.

questions.question: You earn £800 from a small side hustle and have no other self-employed income. Under the trading allowance…
options: You normally don't need to tell HMRC
questions.explanation: Under £1,000 of gross trading income is usually covered by the trading allowance.

questions.question: Checking your own credit score…
questions.explanation: Checking your own score is a soft search. Lenders can't see it and it doesn't affect your score.

questions.question: Hard search vs soft search:
options: A hard search is visible to lenders and can affect your score; a soft one isn't
Soft searches are only for mortgages
questions.explanation: Hard searches happen when you apply for credit. Soft searches include eligibility checks.

questions.question: Being on the electoral roll…
questions.explanation: Lenders use it to confirm your identity and address.

questions.question: “Credit utilisation” means…
options: How much of your available credit you're using
How often you use your card abroad
questions.explanation: High utilisation can make lenders cautious.

questions.question: Credit limit £2,000, balance £1,800. Your utilisation is…
Section 75 protection applies to credit card purchases costing between…
questions.explanation: Section 75 makes the card provider jointly liable for items or services costing £100–£30,000.

questions.question: For a debit card purchase that goes wrong, the route to ask your bank for money back is…
questions.explanation: Chargeback is a card-scheme process, not a legal right, but banks use it routinely.

questions.question: APR shows…
options: The yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and fees
questions.explanation: APR lets you compare the cost of credit.

questions.question: Only paying the minimum on a credit card each month…
options: Makes the debt take much longer and cost far more
questions.explanation: Minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the debt lingers.

questions.question: A 0% balance transfer card usually charges…
options: A one-off fee, often a few percent of the balance
questions.explanation: Check the transfer fee and how long the 0% lasts.

questions.question: You move £3,000 to a 0% card with a 3% transfer fee, and the 0% lasts 20 months. What monthly payment clears it in time?
When a 0% deal ends, any remaining balance…
options: Starts being charged at the normal rate
questions.explanation: Plan to clear it before the deal ends.

questions.question: Missing a credit card payment can…
options: Hurt your credit file and trigger fees
questions.explanation: Set up at least a minimum-payment Direct Debit.

questions.question: What's the main risk with Buy Now Pay Later?
options: It always charges very high interest
It's easy to overspend, and missed payments can mean fees and debt collection
questions.explanation: BNPL feels painless, which makes it easy to stack up repayments.

questions.question: Payday loans are…
options: Among the most expensive ways to borrow
questions.explanation: Their costs are very high even with the cap.

questions.question: Which usually helps build a thin credit file?
options: Using a credit card a little and paying in full every month
Applying for five cards at once
questions.explanation: Small, regular, fully repaid spending shows you manage credit well.

questions.question: A joint account or joint loan with your partner means…
options: Their credit history can affect how lenders see you
Your neighbours are linked to you
questions.explanation: Joint products create a financial association on your files.

questions.question: If you pay your credit card balance in full every month…
options: You still pay interest on purchases
You usually pay no interest on purchases
questions.explanation: Paying in full avoids purchase interest on most cards.

questions.question: How long do missed payments usually stay on a UK credit file?
questions.explanation: Most records stay for six years.

questions.question: A guarantor loan means…
options: Someone else agrees to repay if you can't
questions.explanation: The guarantor is on the hook, so these loans can strain relationships.

questions.question: The 50/30/20 rule splits take-home pay into…
questions.explanation: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings or debt repayment.

questions.question: On £2,000 take-home a month, how much does 50/30/20 say to save?
Which of these is a “need”?
questions.explanation: Needs are essentials such as housing, bills and food.

questions.question: “Pay yourself first” means…
options: Move money to savings as soon as you're paid, before spending
questions.explanation: Saving first means it actually happens.

questions.question: A forgotten £12.99-a-month subscription costs you how much a year?
The quickest way to find forgotten subscriptions is…
options: Check your bank app for recurring payments
questions.explanation: Most banking apps list recurring payments.

questions.question: Saving £5 a day adds up to roughly how much a year?
A sinking fund is…
options: Money saved bit by bit for a known future cost, like an MOT or Christmas
questions.explanation: Sinking funds stop predictable costs becoming surprises.

questions.question: Which is a SMART goal?
options: “Save £600 for a holiday by June by putting away £100 a month”
questions.explanation: It's specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

questions.question: If you spend more than you earn, you have…
questions.explanation: A deficit means money is running out or debt is building.

questions.question: Zero-based budgeting means…
options: Giving every pound of income a job until nothing is unassigned
questions.explanation: Every pound is planned, including savings.

questions.question: Take-home pay £2,200. Rent £900, bills £250, food £300, transport £150. What share goes on these needs?
A good trick against impulse buying is…
options: Buying immediately before the price rises
questions.explanation: A pause lets the urge pass.

questions.question: “Lifestyle creep” is when…
options: Spending rises with your income, so you don't save more
A scam slowly drains your account
questions.explanation: Save part of every pay rise before you get used to it.

questions.question: Pack A: 6 eggs for £1.50. Pack B: 15 eggs for £3.30. Which is cheaper per egg?
questions.explanation: A is 25p per egg, B is 22p.

questions.question: Cereal A: 500g for £2.00. Cereal B: 750g for £2.70. Which is better value?
questions.explanation: A is £4.00/kg, B is £3.60/kg.

questions.question: “Was £5, now £3.50.” What's the discount?
A 4-pack of tins costs £4.00, a single tin 95p. Which is cheaper per tin?
questions.explanation: The 4-pack is £1.00 a tin. Multipacks aren't always cheaper.

questions.question: Shampoo: 400ml for £3.60 on “3 for 2”, or 1 litre for £7.50. You need 1.2 litres. Cheapest way?
questions.explanation: 3 for 2 = £7.20 for 1.2 litres. The other way is £11.10.

questions.question: Coffee: a 200g jar for £5.00 or a 750g bag for £16.50. How much do you save per 100g with the bag?
Shrinkflation is when…
options: The pack shrinks but the price stays the same
questions.explanation: The unit price on the shelf label exposes it.

questions.question: 1,000 loyalty points are worth £10 at the till or £30 with a partner. The partner option is worth…
questions.explanation: Partner rewards can multiply your points' value.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Rights Act, you can reject faulty goods for a full refund within…
questions.explanation: You have a 30-day short-term right to reject faulty goods.

questions.question: Buying online from a UK trader, you usually have a cooling-off period of…
questions.explanation: For most online purchases you can cancel within 14 days. Some items, like personalised goods, are excluded.

questions.question: Buy-one-get-one-free is good value only if…
options: You'll actually use both before they go off
questions.explanation: A free item you bin saves nothing.

questions.question: “Up to 70% off” usually means…
questions.explanation: “Up to” means the biggest discount applies to only a few items.

questions.question: Juice: 500ml for £1.75 or 2 litres for £6.00. Which is cheaper per 100ml?
questions.explanation: 35p vs 30p per 100ml.

questions.question: When are supermarket reductions (yellow stickers) usually biggest?
questions.explanation: Prices often drop further towards closing.

questions.question: You buy a £50 supermarket gift card at 4% off via a cashback app, then pay with it and still earn 1 point per £1 (1 point = 1p). Total saved?
questions.explanation: £2 cashback + 50p in points = £2.50.

questions.question: How does a cashback site make money to pay you?
options: It shares the commission retailers pay it when you buy via its link
questions.explanation: Retailers pay commission and the site passes part of it to you.

questions.question: To make sure cashback tracks, you should…
options: Click through from the cashback site and accept cookies
Buy through the retailer's app directly
questions.explanation: Tracking relies on cookies. Ad blockers and some extensions can break it.

questions.question: Using a voucher code that isn't listed on the cashback site can…
questions.explanation: Many retailers decline cashback when unauthorised codes are used.

questions.question: Cashback marked “pending” means…
options: The retailer hasn't confirmed it yet, which can take weeks
questions.explanation: Pending cashback can still be declined.

questions.question: Which of these commonly gets cashback declined?
questions.explanation: No sale, no commission, no cashback.

questions.question: A £400 laptop: 3% from a cashback site plus 1% from a cashback card. Total back?
Buy a £60 supermarket gift card at 5% back. You earn…
What's a sensible rule with gift card cashback apps?
options: Only buy for shops you'll definitely spend at, and spend it fairly soon
questions.explanation: Unused balances, or a retailer going bust, can lose you money.

questions.question: Why compare two cashback sites before buying?
options: Rates for the same shop can differ
questions.explanation: One site may pay double the other for the same retailer.

questions.question: Cashback is best treated as…
options: A bonus that's only real once it's paid out
questions.explanation: Don't spend it until it lands.

questions.question: Buying something you don't need just to get cashback…
options: Still costs more than not buying it
questions.explanation: 10% back on something you didn't need is still 90% spent.

questions.question: A text claiming to be your bank asks you to reply with a code you just received. You should…
options: Never share it: the code is only for you
questions.explanation: One-time codes are for you only.

questions.question: A stranger offers you £200 to let money pass through your bank account. This is…
questions.explanation: Money mules can be prosecuted and lose their bank accounts.

questions.question: Where can you forward a scam text for free in the UK?
questions.explanation: 7726 spells SPAM on a keypad.

questions.question: A Marketplace seller insists on a bank transfer and refuses PayPal Goods & Services. The main risk?
questions.explanation: Protected payment methods let you get money back if the item never arrives.

questions.question: Authorised Push Payment (APP) fraud is when…
options: You're tricked into sending the money yourself
A bank charges you by mistake
questions.explanation: You make the payment, tricked by someone posing as your bank, a seller or a friend.

questions.question: Which web address is most likely fake?
questions.explanation: Real UK government sites end in .gov.uk.

questions.question: After losing money to a scam, someone offers to recover it for an upfront fee. This is…
questions.explanation: Recovery scams target people who've already been scammed.

questions.question: A caller says they're from your bank and you're unsure. Safest move?
options: Call back the number they gave you
Hang up and call 159 or the number on your card
Ask them to read out your balance
questions.explanation: Scammers can fake caller ID.

questions.question: A website shows a padlock next to its address. That means…
options: Only that the connection is encrypted
questions.explanation: Scam sites can have padlocks too.

questions.question: Your bank will never ask you to…
questions.explanation: “Safe account” requests are always scams.

questions.question: Since October 2024, mandatory reimbursement for APP fraud victims covers most cases up to…
questions.explanation: Banks must reimburse most APP fraud victims up to £85,000, with some exceptions.

questions.question: A “Hi Mum” scam message usually…
options: Comes from a new number asking for urgent money
questions.explanation: Call the real person on their old number first.

questions.question: A text says your parcel has a £1.45 fee to pay via a link. Best move?
options: Treat it as a likely scam and check via the courier's official site
questions.explanation: Small fees are the hook to steal card details.

questions.question: Which is the strongest password habit?
options: Unique passwords or passphrases, a password manager and 2FA
questions.explanation: Reused passwords let one breach unlock everything.

questions.question: Two-factor authentication (2FA) means…
options: A second check, like a code or app approval, on top of your password
questions.explanation: Even if a password leaks, 2FA blocks most break-ins.

questions.question: A QR code sticker on a parking meter could be…
options: A “quishing” scam leading to a fake payment page
questions.explanation: Use the official app or the meter itself where possible.

questions.question: What can happen to someone caught acting as a money mule?
options: Prosecution, bank account closure and years of trouble getting credit
questions.explanation: Consequences can last for years.

questions.question: A ticket seller on social media only accepts bank transfer. Safer option?
options: Use official resale sites, or pay by credit card or PayPal Goods & Services
questions.explanation: Ticket scams thrive on unprotected payments.

questions.question: In the UK, you can report a suspicious email by forwarding it to…
questions.explanation: The National Cyber Security Centre runs this reporting service.

questions.question: Which is a classic romance-scam warning sign?
options: They're happy to video call early on
They never meet in person, have repeated emergencies and ask for money
They introduce you to their friends
questions.explanation: Never send money to someone you've only met online.

questions.question: An investment app shows big gains, but you must pay a “tax” or “fee” before you can withdraw. This is…
questions.explanation: Fake platforms invent fees to squeeze out more money.

questions.question: Refer-a-friend: you get a bonus when a friend joins. Your friend usually…
options: Often gets a bonus too, so check both sides' terms
questions.explanation: Many schemes reward both sides.

questions.question: A legit survey site will never ask you to…
questions.explanation: Paying to join is a red flag.

questions.question: A game app pays £15 if you reach level 30 in 14 days. It takes about 25 hours. Your hourly rate?
questions.explanation: £15 ÷ 25 hours = 60p an hour.

questions.question: A survey site pays 40p per survey with a £5 minimum cash-out. Half your attempts get screened out. Roughly how many attempts to cash out?
questions.explanation: You need 13 completed surveys, so about 25 attempts.

questions.question: Survey A pays £1 for 10 minutes. Survey B pays £2.50 for 30 minutes. Which pays more per hour?
questions.explanation: A is £6/hour, B is £5/hour.

questions.question: Survey sites typically pay…
options: A few pence to a couple of pounds per survey
questions.explanation: It's pocket money for spare minutes.

questions.question: Before putting hours into a rewards app, check…
options: The minimum cash-out and recent payout reviews
questions.explanation: Some apps set cash-outs high enough that few people reach them.

questions.question: What helps you sell unwanted items faster and for more?
options: Clear photos and an honest description
The highest price you can think of
questions.explanation: Good photos and honesty build trust.

questions.question: What's the honest way to share referral codes?
options: Share where the rules allow, never spam or fake reviews
questions.explanation: Spam gets codes banned and communities annoyed.

questions.question: Using fake or duplicate accounts to claim referral bonuses is…
options: Against the terms, can be fraud, and leads to clawbacks or bans
Fine if the amounts are small
questions.explanation: Companies check for duplicate accounts.

questions.question: You miss a play-to-earn milestone deadline by one day. Usually you get…
questions.explanation: Deadlines are strict, so check them before you start.

questions.question: A “mystery shopper” job sends you a cheque to cash, asking you to wire part of it back. This is…
questions.explanation: The cheque bounces later and you lose the money you sent.

questions.question: The energy price cap limits…
options: The unit rates and standing charges on default tariffs
questions.explanation: It caps rates, not your total bill. Use more and you pay more.

questions.question: An energy standing charge is…
options: A fixed daily charge, however much you use
questions.explanation: You pay it even if you use no energy.

questions.question: Who sets the energy price cap?
questions.explanation: Ofgem reviews the cap regularly.

questions.question: When a broadband or mobile contract ends, prices often…
options: Rise unless you renegotiate or switch
questions.explanation: Providers must tell you when your contract ends, so use that to haggle.

questions.question: A SIM-only deal makes the most sense when…
options: You own your phone and don't need a new one
You want a free new phone
questions.explanation: Keeping your phone and going SIM-only is often far cheaper.

questions.question: The council tax discount for a single adult living alone is…
questions.explanation: Adults living alone usually get 25% off.

questions.question: Option 1: a phone contract at £45/month for 24 months. Option 2: buy the phone for £600 plus SIM-only at £12/month. How much does option 2 save over 24 months?
Broadband “social tariffs” are for…
options: People on certain benefits, such as Universal Credit
questions.explanation: They're cheaper packages for eligible households.

questions.question: A water meter often saves money when…
options: Fewer people live in the home than there are bedrooms
questions.explanation: Smaller households often pay less on a meter.

questions.question: Paying for energy by monthly Direct Debit is usually…
options: Cheaper than paying when the bill arrives
questions.explanation: Suppliers usually charge less for Direct Debit.

questions.question: Employers must auto-enrol eligible workers aged 22+ who earn over…
questions.explanation: The auto-enrolment earnings trigger is £10,000 a year.

questions.question: The minimum total auto-enrolment contribution on qualifying earnings is…
questions.explanation: 8% in total, with at least 3% from the employer.

questions.question: The minimum employer contribution under auto-enrolment is…
questions.explanation: Employers must pay at least 3% of qualifying earnings.

questions.question: Opting out of your workplace pension means…
questions.explanation: Opting out gives up money your employer would add for you.

questions.question: Pension tax relief means…
options: The government adds back tax on your contributions
questions.explanation: Contributions get tax relief at your income tax rate, within limits.

questions.question: The normal minimum age to access most private pensions is…
questions.explanation: The minimum pension age is set to rise to 57 in 2028.

questions.question: The State Pension age is 66 and is rising to…
questions.explanation: It's rising to 67 between 2026 and 2028.

questions.question: To get any new State Pension you usually need at least how many qualifying NI years?
questions.explanation: You usually need 10 years for any State Pension and 35 for the full amount.

questions.question: You invest £100 a month for 30 years at 5% a year. Roughly how much do you end up with?
questions.explanation: You pay in £36,000, and compound growth takes it to about £83,000.

questions.question: Most people can take up to what share of their pension tax-free?
questions.explanation: Usually 25%, subject to an overall cap.
questions.verify: Tax-free lump sum rules and cap

questions.question: Lost track of an old workplace pension? Use…
questions.explanation: It's free on gov.uk.

parts.text: Royal Mail: your parcel is on hold
because of an unpaid shipping fee of £1.45.
parts.why: Small surprise fees are a classic hook.

parts.text: Pay within 12 hours
parts.why: A tight deadline is pressure to stop you thinking.

parts.text: or it will be returned to the sender.
royalmail-redelivery-uk.com
parts.why: Not an official Royal Mail address.

investigations.explanation: Check deliveries on the official website or app, never through a link in a text.

parts.text: Dear Customer,
parts.why: A generic greeting instead of your name.

parts.text: after our annual calculation you are owed a tax refund of £468.20.
Claim within 24 hours
parts.why: Urgency again.

parts.text: at hmrc-gov-refunds.net
parts.why: Official HMRC sites end in gov.uk.

parts.text: and enter your card details to receive it.
parts.why: Refunds never need your card details.

parts.text: Kind regards, HM Revenue & Customs.

investigations.explanation: HMRC doesn't send refund links. Forward scam emails to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and texts to 7726.

parts.text: Hello, this is the fraud team at your bank.
We've spotted suspicious payments on your account.
To keep your money safe, move it to a new safe account now,
parts.why: Banks never ask you to move money to a safe account.

parts.text: don't tell anyone, not even staff in your branch,
parts.why: Asking for secrecy is a huge red flag.

parts.text: and read me the code we've just sent to your phone.
parts.why: One-time codes are for you only.

investigations.explanation: Hang up and call 159 or the number on your card, ideally from a different phone.

parts.text: I turned £250 into £8,000 in three weeks!
parts.why: Huge fast returns are the hook.

parts.text: Guaranteed profits, zero risk.
parts.why: No real investment is guaranteed.

parts.text: My account manager trades for you,
just send your deposit in crypto.
parts.why: Crypto payments are almost impossible to recover.

parts.text: Only 5 places left this week!
parts.why: Fake scarcity to rush you.

parts.text: Link in bio.

investigations.explanation: Check firms on the FCA Register and Warning List before investing.

parts.text: Work from home as a Payments Assistant.
Earn £500 a week, no experience needed.
parts.why: High pay for no experience is a warning sign.

parts.text: Receive payments into your own bank account and send them on to our partners,
parts.why: This is money muling, and it's illegal.

parts.text: keeping 10% for yourself.
parts.why: A cut for moving money is how mule recruiters tempt people.

parts.text: Flexible hours.

investigations.explanation: Never let anyone move money through your account.

parts.text: Brand new games console, still sealed.
£120 (normally £450).
parts.why: A price far below normal is the bait.

parts.text: Bank transfer only, no PayPal.
parts.why: Refusing protected payments removes your buyer protection.

parts.text: I'm working abroad, so a courier will deliver it.
parts.why: A seller you can't meet, plus a courier story.

parts.text: Happy to send more photos.

investigations.explanation: Use protected payments and see items in person when you can.

parts.text: MEGA CLEARANCE: 90% off all designer trainers!
parts.why: Unrealistic discounts on brands.

parts.text: Free UK delivery on orders over £50.
Pay by bank transfer for an extra 10% off.
parts.why: Pushing bank transfer means no card protection.

parts.text: Questions? Email shopdeals2026@gmail.com
parts.why: A real retailer uses its own email domain.

parts.text: Returns accepted within 14 days.

investigations.explanation: Check reviews and company details, and pay by card.

parts.text: Hi Mum, I dropped my phone in the bath.
This is my new number.
parts.why: A new number stops you checking with the real person.

parts.text: Can you pay a bill for me today? It's urgent.
parts.why: An urgent money request is the whole point.

parts.text: I can't talk on the phone right now,
parts.why: Avoiding a call stops you hearing it isn't them.

parts.text: love you x

investigations.explanation: Call them on their old number before sending anything.

parts.text: Ofgem: Energy Bill Rebate 2026.
You are entitled to a rebate of £315.
parts.why: Ofgem regulates energy. It doesn't email people rebates.

parts.text: To receive it, confirm your bank details
parts.why: Asking for bank details to “pay” you is a giveaway.

parts.text: before midnight tonight
parts.why: Artificial deadline.

parts.text: via ofgem-rebates-uk.com.
parts.why: Not an official gov.uk or ofgem.gov.uk address.

investigations.explanation: Any genuine energy support comes via your supplier or gov.uk, not a random email.

parts.text: Hi! I'm Sophie from a recruitment agency.
parts.why: Unsolicited job offers on WhatsApp are a common scam opener.

parts.text: We pay £100–£300 a day for liking videos online.
parts.why: Unrealistic pay for trivial tasks.

parts.text: You'll get small payments at first to build trust.
To unlock higher-paying tasks, just top up your account with a deposit.
parts.why: Paying to earn is the core of “task scams”.

parts.text: Reply YES to start.

investigations.explanation: Real employers never ask you to pay to work.

parts.text: Hi, I'd like to buy your sofa. I'll pay full price.
I've sent the money, check your email for the PayPal confirmation.
parts.why: Fake payment emails are used to rush you. Check the PayPal app itself.

parts.text: I accidentally sent £200 too much, please refund the extra by bank transfer.
parts.why: Overpayment refund requests are a classic trick.

parts.text: My courier will collect,
but you need to pay their £50 insurance fee first.
parts.why: Sellers never need to pay a buyer's courier.

investigations.explanation: Only trust payments you can see in your own account or app.

parts.text: ALERT: A new payee “J SMITH” was added to your account.
If this wasn't you,
call us urgently on 0800 046 1234.
parts.why: Never call a number given in an unexpected message. Use the one on your card.

parts.text: Your account will be frozen in 1 hour otherwise.
parts.why: Threats and deadlines are pressure tactics.

parts.text: Do not use your banking app as it may be compromised.
parts.why: Steering you away from your real app is a giveaway.

investigations.explanation: Check your banking app or call 159.

parts.text: PARKING CHARGE NOTICE.
You have parked in a restricted zone.
Pay £60 within 24 hours to avoid a £150 penalty.
parts.why: Extreme urgency is a pressure tactic.

parts.text: Scan the QR code to pay now.
parts.why: QR codes on unexpected notices can lead to fake payment sites.

parts.text: Payments accepted by bank transfer only.
parts.why: Legit operators offer proper payment options.

investigations.explanation: Check the operator independently and pay only through official channels.

parts.text: Your TV Licence Direct Debit has failed.
Your licence will be cancelled today
parts.why: Urgent cancellation threats are typical.

parts.text: unless you update your payment details
at tvlicensing-renewals.co.uk.
parts.why: Check the address carefully. Lookalike domains are common.

parts.text: Dear Valued Customer,
parts.why: Generic greeting.

investigations.explanation: Go to the official site by typing the address yourself.

parts.text: Lovely 2-bed flat in Zone 2, only £700 a month!
parts.why: Rent far below market rate.

parts.text: I'm the landlord but I'm working abroad,
parts.why: An owner who can't show you the property.

parts.text: so I can't show you around.
Send the deposit and first month's rent
parts.why: Paying before viewing is how renters lose money.

parts.text: and I'll post you the keys.

investigations.explanation: Never pay before viewing, and use a protected deposit scheme.

parts.text: Good morning, I'm calling about an exclusive opportunity.
parts.why: Unexpected calls about investments are a major red flag. Pension cold calling is illegal.

parts.text: Our clients earn 12% a year, guaranteed.
parts.why: Guaranteed returns don't exist.

parts.text: We're not on the FCA Register yet because we're so new,
parts.why: Unauthorised firms leave you without protection.

parts.text: but you need to decide today.
parts.why: Pressure to decide now.

parts.text: I'll send you a brochure.

investigations.explanation: Hang up, then check the firm on the FCA Register and Warning List.
